approach:
This assessment evaluated the security and correctness of the AYET token contract using manual review supported by static analysis (Slither) and AI-assisted retrieval over prior audit precedents.
The review emphasised:
- Architecture review and threat modelling of the upgradeable proxy design.
- Privileged-role and centralization analysis.
- Manual verification of token logic against intended behaviour.
- Code quality and best-practice alignment.
This is an AI-assisted internal review intended to support a human reviewer. It is not a certification and does not replace an independent professional audit.

findings.title: Initial Token Distribution
findings.description: The entire fixed supply of 4,000,000,000 AYET is minted to a single `initialReceiver` address during initialization. Concentrating the full supply in one address is a centralization risk: the holder can move or sell tokens without community consensus, and a compromise of that key could allow an attacker to dump the supply on the market, causing severe damage to the project.
findings.recommendation:
Publish a transparent token-distribution plan at a public, community-accessible location. Hold undistributed tokens in a multi-signature wallet (2-of-3 or 3-of-5) rather than a single externally owned account, and restrict access to deployer keys.
Additional measures:
- Lock up a portion of tokens and release them on a vesting schedule.
- Consider third-party KYC of the team to increase accountability.
- Provide the distribution-plan URL and the multisig address so status can be verified.

findings.title: Centralized Control Of Contract Upgrade
findings.description: AYETToken is a UUPS-upgradeable contract whose implementation can be replaced by the `onlyOwner` role via `_authorizeUpgrade`. A single owner key can therefore change the logic behind the proxy. If that key is compromised, an attacker could point the proxy at a malicious implementation and introduce arbitrary behaviour.
findings.recommendation:
Restrict access to the upgrade authority using a combination of a timelock and a multi-signature wallet, and notify the community before any upgrade.
Short Term:
- Assign the upgrade role to a multi-signature (2-of-3 / 3-of-5) wallet.
- Add a timelock with reasonable latency (e.g. 48 hours) on upgrades.
- Publish the timelock and signer addresses.
Long Term:
- Introduce a DAO / governance module to control upgrades.
Permanent:
- Renounce ownership or remove the upgrade functionality once the contract is final.

findings.title: Centralization Related Risks
findings.description:
The owner holds several privileged functions: `pause()` / `unpause()`, `transferOwnership()`, `renounceOwnership()`, and `upgradeToAndCall()` (UUPS, gated by `_authorizeUpgrade` with `onlyOwner`). No on-chain timelock, multisig, or role separation is enforced inside AYETToken.
Because `_update()` is protected by `whenNotPaused`, a compromised owner could immediately halt all transfers, burns, and other balance-changing operations, then resume, transfer, or renounce ownership. More importantly, the UUPS upgrade authority lets the owner replace the implementation with arbitrary logic — including new minting, blacklisting, confiscation, or permanent-freeze behaviour.
In the current implementation the owner cannot directly mint or seize balances, but the upgrade authority makes those restrictions non-binding in practice, concentrating strong trust in the owner key.
findings.recommendation:
Apply the same tiered controls as for the upgrade authority, and carefully manage the privileged key.
Short Term:
- Timelock (e.g. 48h) plus multi-signature (2-of-3 / 3-of-5) on privileged operations.
Long Term:
- Timelock combined with a DAO / governance module for decentralization and transparency.
Permanent:
- Renounce ownership or remove the risky functions once no longer needed.
